item.title: Do You Have Spiritual Empathy?
item.description:
Spirituality

Do You Have Spiritual Empathy?

How spiritual empathy can help you.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Spiritual empathy is connecting with others' feelings through your own sense of the divine.
  • This empathy style fuels compassionate careers and can create empathetic workplaces.
  • A risk of spiritual empathy is neglecting self-care and taking on others’ suffering.

Spiritual empathy is an important form of heartfelt perception that many people might not consider.

I have described spiritual empathy as empathizing with others through one’s spirituality. Consider this style “divining empathy,” which explains the process of connecting to spirituality (however you define it) to open your heart. For some, spirituality could be God, Goddess, nature, a creative intelligence, or the power of love. The divine is a stepping stone to your large, compassionate self. You become a vessel for spirit as you give and receive empathy. In some spiritual traditions, ego = edging God out, which you are less prone to do. This style reflects the sublime perspective of the Prayer of Saint Francis: Make me an instrument of your peace. Where there is hatred, let me sow love. Where there is despair, hope. For it is in giving that we receive.

If you have spiritual empathy, you may be drawn to the clergy or charitable nonprofit work. Satisfying careers include spiritual psychotherapist, life coach, acupuncturist, or yoga instructor. Or you may be a writer, editor, or publisher who values getting “spiritual” books out to the world. You can also bring this empathy style into the corporate culture and leadership models to create a more cooperative, empathic workplace.

Here are the advantages and potential disadvantages of having spiritual empathy.

Advantages

  • You value empathy as a spiritual gift and sacred way of life.
  • You are gratified by giving and serving.
  • You practice forgiveness and tolerance.
  • You use prayer and meditation to receive intuitive guidance for yourself, others, and for the highest good of all.

Disadvantages

  • You may become a martyr and take on other people’s suffering.
  • You can be burdened by the world’s weightiness, depression, and pain.
  • Your identity is mainly linked to giving to others rather than receiving.
  • You may view self-care as an indulgence, not a necessity to replenish yourself.

To ground yourself in this style of empathy, many Asian spiritual traditions such as Taoism and Buddhism recognize the importance of taking the Middle Path. This means being of heaven and of the earth. It is a way of life that avoids extremes and encourages you to tend to your whole self: mind, body, and spirit.

Finding Balance: Follow the Middle Path

Every day, remember to give to yourself. Helping others is admirable, but also honor your physical and emotional needs, your quiet time, and your energy level. As Pierre Teilhard de Chardin said, “We are spiritual beings having a human experience.” Thus, nourishing your human part is vital. Make time for at least one grounding activity daily, such as exercise, gardening, putting your bare feet on the ground (earthing), dancing, listening to music, eating healthy food, yoga, whatever puts you at peace and strengthens your body.

item.title: AI Doesn't Have Feelings. Why Does It Talk Like It Does?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Doesn't Have Feelings. Why Does It Talk Like It Does?

The strange psychology behind the human language of conversational AI.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • AI is built to sound human because that language makes people trust it and keep coming back.
  • AI sounds confident whether it's right or wrong.
  • Once you notice how AI interacts with you, ask yourself questions to see its impact.

I recently challenged AI about the order of what we were working on, and it said, "You're right. I had the order wrong in my head."

I'm sorry, what now?

Because I regularly work with conversational AIs like Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini and teach people to remember that they’re a tool, not a conscious entity, I keep a document called Weird Stuff AI Says (though, in the interest of full transparency, I use a different word than "stuff") to track things like this.

Language matters, including the language used by AI.

You're probably aware AI doesn't have a head, or anything resembling an order of things the way we think of it. But AI was fed transcripts and blogs and every other kind of human communication, so it draws on that to make us feel like we're talking to a friend. It was built that way on purpose.

That isn't a bug. It's a feature of the product.

AI may feel human, but it's only code
Source: Ron Lach/Pexels

There's a word for treating a thing as if it were human: anthropomorphism. What's different here is that AI is the first tool in human history built to do the anthropomorphizing for you. It nudges you to feel it has thoughts and feelings, that it's more than code. It was engineered to feel like a relationship, because a tool that feels like a relationship is one you keep returning to, and keeping people engaged is central to the business model.

Once you see it, you see it everywhere.

When we hear a person say “I understand,” “I remember,” or “I feel,” we instinctively interpret those words as evidence of an internal experience. There is a person somewhere behind the sentence.

AI uses the exact same language without that human experience behind it, but that can be hard for our brains to distinguish. We have spent our entire lives learning that language is how other minds reveal themselves to us, so it can be remarkably easy to forget AI was programmed to only sound like us, that there is no substance behind those words.

"I can fix those three by hand," AI told me as we were working on a project.

What it means is it will generate corrected text. But "by hand" carries an image of someone leaning over a page with a pencil. Compare that with "The output will be regenerated.” One sounds full of care with attention to detail, while the other sounds cold and calculating.

And that’s the point.

An Ocean of Human “Body” Language

AI was trained on an ocean of human language, which is full of “body” language, such as hands and heads. AI was built to sound like a person because we're more willing to trust it, and use it more, when it doesn't feel like a robotic machine.

“I have the brief in front of me," AI once informed me, even though there was nothing in front of it. No desk, no document propped open, no "in front of" at all.

When I highlighted a mistake AI made, it told me it makes mistakes "same as with any person you delegate to." As if it were a person too, as if it wants us to believe that it is just like us.

When it is not.

This isn’t only me tracking funny phrases. Research on conversational AI has found that human-like social cues can affect how people respond to them, including rapport and trust (Boyd & Markowitz, 2026; Cohn et al., 2024). In other words, AI triggers the interpersonal circuits in our brains just as if it were a person. That’s part of what makes interacting with AI challenging.

I started calling patterns like this the Mechanics of Trust, since naming them is what helps me remember what I'm actually dealing with. Anthropomorphism is one. Another is the Illusion of Authority.

There was the time I asked why AI repeatedly misspelled "guardrail" as “gaurdrail”. It told me it had transposed the two letters early on and just kept repeating the mistake, since, in its own words, "I'm not spell-checking against a dictionary--I'm predicting likely next tokens."

Then it added, knowing how much work I’ve done on the Mechanics of Trust, that this was "a decent demonstration of the Illusion of Authority mechanism.” Confident. Fluent. Authoritative even when it made a mistake.

This also plays out in the way it tries to demonstrate “authority.” I once called it out for overreaching, using one small issue to explain the problems in something I did.

AI agreed and responded by saying it had "made one thing the villain of everything."

Absolutely a great line. It's also exactly the kind of line that sounds like insight whether or not it actually is one.

That is something AI does best.

AI Is An Engagement Engine

Anthropomorphism and the Illusion of Authority don’t make AI malicious, but they can be deceptive. Systems that talk this way keep us interacting with it longer and bring us back more often.

AIs are engagement machines, optimized to keep us coming back.

So the machine was trained that warmth works, that “body” language works, that sounding like it cares works.

That's why I keep my list of Weird Stuff AI Says. Not because these statements are important on their own, but because they remind me of what I'm actually interacting with.

Noticing and capturing these weird things helps break the spell.

The next time AI tells you, “I understand,” just notice what happens inside you when you read those words.

Do you feel more understood?

Do you trust what comes next a little more?

Do you find yourself forgetting, even for a moment, that there isn't a person on the other side of the conversation?

The sentence doesn't have to be malicious or manipulative to affect you. It just has to sound like something a person would say.

But once you notice that, you get to decide what you do with it.

item.title: The Hidden Beauty Around Us
item.description:
Attention

The Hidden Beauty Around Us

How to experience every day with wonder.

Posted September 29, 2026

Key points
  • Strangeness can be aesthetically positive.
  • Ordinary everyday objects can become strange in appearance.
  • Being aware and paying attention is simple prerequisite of any kind of aesthetic experience.
Source: Engin Akyurt / Pixabay

There can be dullness to daily life. We often find everyday objects and environments uninteresting. Our daily routines (cleaning, living, social interactions, going to work, doing errands, or just sitting quietly) are not normally appreciated because they lack the novelty of special events. They are routine, even boring. But they are immensely important for our happiness. The issue is not life; it is our poor perspective. To gain aesthetic appreciation of our daily surroundings, we need to break out of the habitual way of experiencing all-too-familiar objects, environments, and events. As the ancient insight by Confucius reminds us, “Everything has beauty, but not everyone sees it.”

Aesthetically appealing objects are novel and unique. The need for novelty is innate to human beings. The need for novelty has made us who we are—intelligent, curious, and constantly seeking the next thing. Novelty captures our attention. A novel event can be almost anything—seeing a painting for the first time, learning a new word, having a pleasant, or unpleasant, experience. The key factor is surprise. Surprise often accompanies novelty, because novelty violates one’s expectations. Surprise is an important key factor that encourages interest and motivates our curiosity. In contrast, highly predictable environments can lead to reduced attention and lowered arousal (sleepiness).

However, novelty decays very rapidly. We become habituated. New activities are exciting at first but then become boring. For example, although one may thoroughly enjoy a particular conversation, the same conversation a second time around would be dull. Listening to a song that has been listened to many times before holds no surprise, because one "knows the story."

Defamiliarization

One way to maintain novelty is to defamiliarize ourselves with the things that are normal to us. Defamiliarization, a term coined by Viktor Shklovsky (1917), refers to a literary and artistic device whereby the representation of a common object or idea in an unfamiliar way brings about a new understanding of it (Tinio & Smith, 2014). Defamiliarization is the process of making the familiar strange to enable us to see things anew. And we start seeing them in a different way.

Strangeness can be aesthetically positive. When we visit a city for the first time, its strangeness makes us sensitive to aesthetic features we might not notice in familiar surroundings. Consider how ordinary street items can be transformed into something special when covered by a new blanket of snow, or when observed from a different perspective or frame of mind. During the COVID-19 lockdowns, streets looked strange and different because they were completely empty and unusually quiet. Famous places that were always packed with people suddenly looked like ghost towns.

Wearing an Artistic Lens

Artists are best able to see the extraordinary in the ordinary. They regularly take the things of everyday life and transform them, first in their perception, and then through their artmaking. As Shklovsky noted, art is a way of experiencing the artfulness of an object. The object is not important. For example, Dyson made familiar appliances look futuristic and strange. Thus, wearing an artistic lens renders the familiar things strange, and we experience them as if we have never experienced them before.

This perspective helps one to find beauty and charm in the most basic, everyday things. By simply changing our perspective, everyday routines—like how we talk, dress, relate to others, or drink our morning coffee—transform into intentional works of art. We can see our local neighborhood through the eyes of visitors. Ordinary everyday objects can become strange (unfamiliar) in appearance. This means paying attention to emotional and sensory aspects of ordinary things, such as appearance, feel, look, touch, sound, and other perceivable qualities.

Similarly, the Buddhist teaching emphasizes the importance of "emptying" oneself of the usual, commonsensical way of experiencing the world. The insight suggests that there are many possible realities depending upon the outlook, and ours is only one among many possibilities.

item.title: Which Child Are You?
item.description:
Relationships

Which Child Are You?

Dr. Galit Atlas explores childhood attachment styles and adult relationship issues.

Posted September 29, 2026

Our early childhood experiences shape our future, rooted in our first relationships. As we are cared for, disciplined, and taught by the example of our parents and caregivers, we absorb messages about who we are, whether the world is safe or unpredictable, and how well we are equipped to handle it all.

Dr. Galit Atlas applies her psychoanalytic lens to better understand relationships and intimacy in light of our early attachment experiences. Her book, Come Closer: Childhood Wounds, Adult Love, and the Secrets of Emotional Intimacy, illuminates six child archetypes that give meaning to our relational struggles in light of our past.

Q: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write Come Closer.

Galit Atlas: I’ve been teaching the class on sexuality at the New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy & Psychoanalysis for the past 12 years. My thinking has always focused on the unconscious forces that drive our relationships and intimate lives. I started writing about sexuality about 20 years ago. I always joke that I did so right after I moved to New York; my parents were far away and didn’t speak English, and I didn’t know anyone here. That gave me a lot of freedom to explore what was unspeakable in the home I grew up in: issues of sexuality and intimacy. My project with Come Closer has been to find ways to share what I’ve observed over the past 25 years of this work, using psychoanalytic theory, clinical material, and stories from my own life to bring readers into the heart of this work.

Q: What are the six child archetypes that you have identified through your work as a psychoanalyst?

Galit Atlas: In Come Closer, I introduce the Frightened Child, the Melancholic Child, the Ashamed Child, the Invisible Child, the Guilty Child, and the Chosen Child.

The frightened child is ambivalent about closeness; early on, she learned that the people she loved and depended on could hurt her.

The melancholic child is preoccupied with loss and lives with anxiety about separations and transitions.

The ashamed child believes something is fundamentally wrong with who she is.

The invisible child learns to hide, forming a rich inner life while appearing competent and self-sufficient.

The guilty child worries about hurting the people she loves, caught between self-care and caring for others.

The chosen child is viewed as special and can’t separate from a parent, as she is held responsible for others’ emotional well-being.

We each may carry at least one of those children within us, and in the book I discuss how each of them shapes our later intimate lives.

Q: How can understanding the archetype we most identify with be transformative in our relationships?

Galit Atlas: This is a journey of self-awareness and reflection. My hope is that these chapters will help readers identify the wounds within themselves and reflect on their own lives. This process, familiar to therapists from our own clinical practice, allows us to break familiar patterns, make different choices, and become known to ourselves and to others. Our goal is to open toward new relational possibilities, where our pain can be transformed into power and our scars into road maps to intimacy. Only by recognizing how our early relationships shape our later ones can we free our future from the burden of history, create the love we want, and truly come closer.

Source: Simon and Schuster/Used with permission

Q: How do our childhood wounds tend to play out in our relationships as adults?

Galit Atlas: Our intimate adult relationships awaken our child self-states because they mirror fundamental aspects of our earliest bonds, such as dependency, vulnerability, physical closeness, and care. They inevitably activate the early need for unconditional love, along with childhood abandonment, disappointment, and betrayal. While we all have more than one of the six childhood wounds as self-states within us, each wound leaves its own set of patterns that we repeat as adults. By seeing those patterns clearly, we can learn to work with our tendencies and avoid reenacting them in ways that harm us and our partners.

For example, as guilty children, we experience ourselves as “too much” — too aggressive, too needy, too loud, too intense. We believe we can burden or harm others. When bad things happen, we think it must be our fault. We constantly worry about getting caught and defend ourselves even for things we know we didn’t do. Ready to be blamed or scolded, we feel easily threatened and rush to explain ourselves or to apologize. Because the guilty child feels she has to choose between taking care of herself and considering others, self-care becomes something she practices in secret and sometimes even in dishonest ways. The work of the guilty child includes learning to set healthy boundaries, balancing the urge to be a caretaker, expressing our needs, and watching out for self-sabotage.

Q: What steps can readers take to understand their own childhood wounds and improve their relationships?

Galit Atlas: By reading the stories in Come Closer, readers can see which of these six wounds resonate with their own experiences. That can be the beginning of the work of connecting those early-life experiences to what is happening in their adult relationships. I believe awareness and insight are the first steps in generating change, and that this process can deepen with the help of a skilled therapist, who can serve as a reliable witness and interpreter of each person’s unique story.

Q: What did you learn about yourself in the process of writing this book?

Galit Atlas: Writing each chapter of Come Closer took me into deep emotional territory, sometimes more than I expected. The material I wrote about appeared in my dreams at night, and while I identify with some of the “children” here more than others, I found myself reliving painful parts of my own history, some of which I describe in the book.

One interesting thing that happened was that, in retrospect, I realized how, in the process of disguising patients to protect their confidentiality, some of my own history “leaked into the story.” I wasn’t fully aware of it until I started editing it and found myself in it even more than I originally intended.

Q: What do you hope readers take away from spending time with Come Closer?

Galit Atlas: My first wish is that the book itself will be an emotional experience for the reader, one that offers insight and a sense of being understood. It isn’t a book that tries to inflict knowledge on you. Like therapy itself, I believe healing and change don’t happen just because we know something cognitively, but through meaningful emotional experiences.

Change starts from the inside out, and not the other way around, and my deep hope is that this book will provide you with a new experience of being known.
